title: Motion in a Plane — Class Slides
subject: NIOS Senior Secondary Physics

slides.title: Motion in a Plane
bullets: NIOS Senior Secondary Physics
Class 12 — Chapter 4
Vectors, projectiles, circles, relative velocity
slides.speaker_notes: Open with a quick ball throw across the room to plant the question: what controls range and hang-time? Set up the chapter as the language (vectors) plus three classic problems (projectiles, circular motion, relative velocity).

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Tell a vector from a scalar and resolve any vector into components.
Add two vectors using the triangle / parallelogram law.
Find T, H, R for any projectile and read the trajectory equation.
Compute centripetal acceleration and force; name the source of F_c in real scenarios.
Solve river-crossing and crosswind problems with relative velocity.
slides.speaker_notes: Share these as the takeaways. Promise that by the end every student should be able to do each of these without looking back at notes.

slides.title: Scalars vs vectors
bullets: Scalar: magnitude + unit only (mass, speed, energy).
Vector: magnitude + direction (displacement, velocity, force).
Vectors are drawn as arrows; length = magnitude, orientation = direction.
Two vectors are equal only if magnitudes AND directions agree.
Unit vectors î, ĵ, k̂ point along x, y, z and have magnitude 1.
slides.speaker_notes: Press the point that a vector has no 'home position' — it can be slid parallel to itself anywhere on the page.

slides.title: Vector addition & resolution
bullets: Triangle law: tail-to-head; resultant from free tail to free head.
Parallelogram law: same picture drawn as a parallelogram.
Magnitude: R² = A² + B² + 2 A B cos θ.
Direction: tan α = (B sin θ) / (A + B cos θ).
Resolution: A_x = A cos θ, A_y = A sin θ — turns 2D into two 1Ds.
slides.speaker_notes: Stress that resolution is the trick that makes everything in the chapter tractable. Component-wise we can use the 1D kinematic equations we already know.

slides.title: Example — resultant of 6 N and 8 N at 90°
bullets: Given: A = 6 N, B = 8 N, θ = 90°.
tan α = 8 / 6 ⇒ α ≈ 53° from A.
Could also write as 6î + 8ĵ; magnitude √(36+64) = 10.
slides.speaker_notes: Two ways of getting the same answer — cosine rule and components. Pick the one that's faster in each problem.

slides.title: Projectile motion
bullets: Under gravity alone (no air resistance).
u_x = u cos θ (constant); u_y = u sin θ (changing under g).
Trajectory: y = x tan θ − g x² / (2 u² cos² θ) — a parabola.
T = 2u sin θ / g,  H = u² sin² θ / (2g),  R = u² sin 2θ / g.
Range maximum at θ = 45°.
slides.speaker_notes: Tie back to the opening demo — 30° vs 60° at the same speed give the same range, but very different times in the air.

slides.title: Example — projectile at 20 m/s at 30°
slides.speaker_notes: Walk through this slowly the first time. Then ask students to redo it for θ = 60° and notice that T and H differ but R is the same.

slides.title: Uniform circular motion
bullets: Constant SPEED on a circle; velocity direction keeps changing.
Centripetal acceleration a_c = v² / r = ω² r, points toward centre.
Centripetal force F_c = m v² / r — direction: toward centre.
F_c is NOT a new force — it is supplied by tension / friction / gravity etc.
No outward force in the lab frame; the outward 'feel' is inertia.
slides.speaker_notes: Demo with the string. Ask: 'if I let go, where does the stone go?' Tangentially — not radially outward.

slides.title: Example — car on a flat curve
bullets: Mass 1000 kg, radius 50 m, speed 15 m/s, μ = 0.5.
Required F_c = m v² / r = 4500 N.
Available friction = μ m g = 5000 N.
4500 < 5000 ⇒ car turns safely; v_max = √(μ g r) = √250 ≈ 15.8 m/s.
slides.speaker_notes: Connect this to why icy roads are dangerous in turns — μ collapses and the available friction drops below F_c.

slides.title: Relative velocity in 2D
bullets: v_AB = v_A − v_B — a vector subtraction.
River crossing — shortest TIME: head straight across.
River crossing — shortest PATH: head upstream, sin θ = v_r / v_b.
Crosswind: pilot crabs into the wind to fly straight.
slides.speaker_notes: Real pilots and boat captains do this every day. Tie it back to the vector resolution slide — same idea, different scenario.

slides.title: Quick check — 30 seconds each
bullets: Q1. Which is a vector — mass / energy / displacement / temperature?
Q2. At what angle is the projectile range maximum on level ground?
Q3. The centripetal force on a satellite is supplied by ____.
Q4. Two angles that give the same range as θ are θ and ____.
Q5. v_AB = ____ in terms of v_A and v_B.
slides.speaker_notes: Cold-call quickly. Get the whole class engaged — make sure the answers are: displacement / 45° / gravity / (90°−θ) / v_A − v_B.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Resolve any 2D vector into components — that's how we tame 2D problems.
Constant-a 2D motion = two independent 1D problems linked only by time.
Projectile: parabolic path; T, H, R follow from the components.
UCM: accelerated motion at constant speed; a_c = v² / r toward centre.
Relative velocity in 2D is just a vector subtraction.
Same method everywhere: choose frame → decompose → recompose.
slides.speaker_notes: Close by repeating the method line — that single recipe is the chapter's biggest gift to the rest of physics.
